newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing group disappointed with Nationwide.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing group disappointed with Nationwide.

text.p: A U.S. housing group that claims Nationwide Insurance discriminates against minorities said it was disappointed in the measures announced Friday by the insurer.
Nationwide said it will change its underwriting guidelines to enhance its product offerings to owners of older and less expensive homes and will invest $3 million in urban areas.
"We're really pretty disappointed because what they kept in place was their geographic-based marketing program," said Shanna Smith, executive director of the National Fair Housing Alliance.
"We see that as the real foundation of the company's redlining practices," she said. "This marketing strategy is designed to discourage agents from doing business in urban areas," she said.
She also said she was disappointed in the size of the investment Nationwide plans to make in urban areas.
American Family Insurance Co in 1995 agreed to settle a discrimination suit and provide $14.5 million in low-interest mortgages and other compensation to predominantly black areas of Milwaukee.
But, she said, she believes the problems at Nationwide are more serious than they were at American Family.
"This company is doing too little too late," Smith said.

Richard Crabtree, president of Nationwide's property and casualty insurance companies, categorically denied that the company has engaged in discriminatory practices and said the changes announced by the company demonstrate its commitment to the urban markets.

"While we certainly have not been -- and there is no citable evidence that we have been -- involved in any type of discriminatory practices in these markets, we believe that this initiative certainly represents clearly to everyone at Nationwide and hopefully to the marketplace that we're committed and continue to be committed to that market," Crabtree said.
Under the changes to the underwriting guidelines announced by Nationwide, the company will eliminate restrictions on the age and minimum market value of properties Nationwide will insure.
In addition, Crabtree said replacement cost coverage will now be available to all Nationwide customers.
These initiatives, Crabtree said, are the first step of a broad expansion of the company's efforts in the urban areas.
He said the company plans to increase its presence in other cities and said these initiatives are building on an already substantial presence in the urban markets.
In addition, he said Nationwide's discussions with the Justice Department have been "constructive and positive" and he said he believes these initiatives are responsive to the department's concerns.
